description_full: Starbucks Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as a roaster, marketer, and retailer of coffee internationally. The company operates through three segments: North America, International, and Channel Development. Its stores offer coffee, tea, and other beverages, roasted whole beans and ground coffees, complementary food, packaged coffees, single-serve products, and ready-to-drink beverages; and various food products, such as pastries, breakfast sandwiches, and lunch items. The company also licenses its trademarks through licensed stores, and grocery and foodservice accounts. The company offers its products under the Starbucks Coffee, Teavana, Seattle's Best Coffee, Ethos, and Starbucks Reserve brands. Starbucks Corporation was founded in 1971 and is based in Seattle, Washington.

financial_summary: Starbucks Corporation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $120.2B market cap on $37.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 65% against a 9% cost of capital — a 56-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $2.4B in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.56× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.4×.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.96x).
It accounts for 0.7% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 20% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.46 vs 5y 0.97), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $677.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash, 40% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $50.00 (margin of safety -111%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 2%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $32.69 to $74.91 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 47.7 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 24.3 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 49.2 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 108% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 29 covering analysts target $111 on average, 5% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 65% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 56pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.75).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.56x, but high accruals (-9.0% of assets).
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($3.9B of cash against $16.1B of debt), with interest covered 5.4x.
The current ratio of 0.72 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.9% over 3 years, 9.6% over 5 years and 6.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 84.5% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 6.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 13.5% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 87%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (11 sales, net $1.8M sold).
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (2.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 143% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: CEO pay is $11.1M, and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
